summary:
Problem
Space education for kids is often too abstract (posters, facts) or too technical. Students rarely see the real decisions behind a mission, like sharing limited power between life support, radiation protection, and science.

Solution
Moon Outpost is a browser game where kids aged 7-12 run a Moon base for 10 days. Each day they split fixed power (100, or 70 at lunar night) between three jobs:

Air machine: makes oxygen (the crew uses 25 per day; about 42 power keeps it steady)
Shield: radiation protection. It leaks daily, so charge it before storms
Science: earns points, but gives no air or protection

No choice is free: more shield means less science or air. If oxygen or crew health hits zero, the mission fails.

Solar storms
Two real historical solar storms (NASA DONKI, saved in the game as archived data) hit on random days. A warning comes 2 days ahead, matching the real delay between a flare and its CME reaching its target. A weak shield on arrival costs the crew health. Each storm brings a report and a “Did you know?” fact. Random events make every game different, so kids can try new strategies and learn from failure without harsh punishment.

What players learn
Power is limited, radiation protection must be prepared before a storm, life support comes first, and space weather can be forecast.
details:
What it does and how it works
Moon Outpost is a browser game for kids aged 7-12. Players run a Moon base for 10 days. Each day they get limited power (100 on sunny days, 70 during the lunar night) and split it between three jobs: the air machine (makes oxygen), the shield (radiation protection), and science (earns points). The crew uses 25 oxygen a day, and the shield slowly leaks charge, so no choice is free: more shield means less science or less air. Two solar storms hit on random days. The player gets a warning 2 days ahead, matching the real delay between a solar flare and its particle cloud reaching its target. If the shield is too weak when the storm arrives, the crew loses health. After each storm, the player sees a short report and a “Did you know?” fact. If oxygen or crew health reaches zero, the mission fails.

Benefits
Kids experience a real mission-planning trade-off instead of reading about it. The game needs no download or account and works on phones and computers. Failing is gentle: the report explains what happened and the player can try a new strategy.

Intended impact
We want a young player to walk away understanding three real ideas: power in space is limited, radiation protection must be ready before a storm, and space weather can be forecast. It can also be used in classrooms or by older siblings and parents as a conversation starter about how real missions are planned.

NASA data used

  • NASA DONKI: five real past solar flares are used as the storm events (saved in the game as archived data, not live).
  • NASA OSDR RadLab: the idea that radiation on the International Space Station is higher than on Earth, shown in “Did you know?” cards.
  • NASA OSDR: background on how spaceflight affects astronaut health, behind the “crew health” meter.
    All sources are credited inside the game with links.

Tools and technology
HTML, CSS, and JavaScript in a single web page, with no external frameworks. Edited and tested in Visual Studio Code. Hosted on Netlify and AntiDeploy. We used Claude (an AI assistant by Anthropic) to help plan the game design and write and refine the code and presentation, and we tested and checked the result ourselves.

Creativity
Instead of a quiz, the lesson is the mechanic itself. The warning delay copies how real space weather forecasts work, and storm events and arrival days change every game, so players can replay and test new strategies. We used simple language, big + and − buttons, emoji icons, and a one-line explanation under each job.

Factors we considered

  • Only three resources, so young players are not overwhelmed.
  • No “safe” option: every choice costs something.
  • Plain language for ages 7-12, and an option to explain terms in context.
  • Mobile-friendly design, with reduced motion supported.
  • Honesty about data: the storms are real but archived, and the game balance numbers (such as shield charge needed) are our own design, scaled for kids.
  • Future work: a live DONKI connection, a Mars site, real RadLab dose values, more event types, and a classroom mode.
